**MEMO: Hardware Expansion vs. Utilisation — Recommendation and Reasoning**

**From:** Engineering Lead
**To:** Platform Team
**Re:** Should we buy more GPUs or get better at using the ones we have?

---

I've been sitting with this question for about three weeks now, and I think I've arrived at a position I can defend, though not one I'd stake my reputation on. I want to lay out my reasoning honestly, including the parts where I'm uncertain, because I think the team deserves to see the shape of the argument rather than just its conclusion.

Here's where we are. We own four A100 80GB cards and two H100s. Our average GPU utilisation across the last quarter has hovered around 34 percent, with a long tail of idle hours on weekends and during the overnight window when nobody is running experiments. Meanwhile, the inference team has been asking for more capacity, and the fine-tuning group has been queueing jobs for hours on end. The instinct in the room has been to buy more hardware, and I understand why. It feels like the obvious move, the one that makes the pain go away without requiring anyone to change their habits.

But I want to push back gently, and I want to do it by thinking through what we're actually buying when we buy hardware versus what we're actually buying when we invest in utilisation.

The cost question is the one people reach for first, and it's the one that most clearly favours the utilisation path. A single H100 runs roughly thirty thousand dollars, and that's before we account for the power draw, the cooling infrastructure, the rack space, and the operational overhead of managing another node. If we can lift our average utilisation from 34 percent to 60 percent through better scheduling, smarter batching, and a shared queue with priority tiers, we effectively get the equivalent of two additional H100s for the cost of a few weeks of engineering time. That's not a rounding error. That's the difference between a capital expenditure that locks us into a depreciation schedule and a process improvement that compounds.

Latency is where the argument gets more nuanced, and where I think the case for buying hardware is strongest. Our inference workloads are sensitive to queue depth. When the fine-tuning group saturates the A100s with long-running training jobs, inference requests that should return in under two hundred milliseconds start waiting behind them. No amount of clever scheduling fully eliminates that tension when you're running heterogeneous workloads on the same physical cards. If we buy dedicated inference hardware, we get isolation, and isolation gives us predictable latency. That's real, and I don't want to wave it away.

Reliability cuts both ways. More hardware means more failure domains, which sounds bad, but it also means we can absorb a single card failure without halting everything. Right now, if one of our A100s goes down, we lose a quarter of our training capacity overnight. That's a fragile position. On the other hand, the more hardware we own, the more we're responsible for patching, monitoring, and replacing, and our team is small enough that every hour spent on infrastructure is an hour not spent on the product.

This brings me to opportunity cost, which I think is the most important frame here. Every dollar we spend on hardware is a dollar we don't spend on hiring, on tooling, on the features our customers are asking for. And every engineering week we spend building a better scheduler is a week we don't spend shipping. The question isn't whether utilisation work is free; it isn't. It's whether the return on that engineering time is higher than the return on capital spent on GPUs. I believe it is, at least for now, because we're so far from the utilisation frontier. We're leaving obvious gains on the table.

Reversibility is the final consideration, and it's the one that tips me. Buying hardware is a slow, expensive, semi-permanent commitment. We can't easily sell GPUs back at a good price, and we can't un-buy the operational complexity they introduce. Improving utilisation is reversible in a way that hardware purchases are not. If we build a better scheduling system and it turns out we still need more cards, we can buy them then, and we'll be buying them with better information about what we actually need. If we buy now and discover the bottleneck was always scheduling, we've spent thirty thousand dollars to learn something we could have learned for free.

My recommendation is this: we commit to a six-week utilisation sprint. We build a proper job queue with priority levels, we implement dynamic batching for inference, we set up resource quotas so no single team can monopolise the cluster, and we instrument everything so we can see where the real bottlenecks are. At the end of six weeks, we reconvene with data. If latency is still unacceptable or if we've genuinely saturated the hardware, we buy. But we buy with evidence, not with anxiety.

I'll be honest about my uncertainty here. I could be wrong about how much headroom exists in our current setup. The inference team's latency requirements might be tighter than I'm modelling, and the scheduling work might be harder than it looks. If that's the case, we'll know within a few weeks, and the cost of being wrong is six weeks of engineering time rather than thirty thousand dollars of sunk capital. That asymmetry is what makes this the right bet to make first.

**MEMO**

**From:** Engineering Lead
**To:** Platform & ML Infrastructure Team
**Re:** Local AI Hardware — Procurement vs. Utilisation
**Date:** June 2025

---

I want to put a decision in front of us that has been circling informally for a few weeks: should we purchase additional local GPU capacity, or should we invest the next quarter in squeezing more throughput from the cluster we already own? I have been thinking about this carefully, and I want to lay out my reasoning before we discuss it on Thursday.

The case for buying more hardware is intuitive. We are seeing queue times on inference jobs stretch past acceptable thresholds during peak hours, and the team has been fielding complaints from product engineers who feel blocked. More GPUs would relieve that pressure almost immediately. Latency would become predictable again, and the psychological relief of not rationing compute would be real. There is also a reliability argument: additional nodes give us redundancy, so a single hardware failure no longer cascades into a full-day outage for the team.

But I want us to be honest about what we actually know about our current utilisation. The numbers I have seen suggest we are running at roughly 40 to 55 percent average GPU utilisation across the cluster, with significant variance depending on the time of day and the workload mix. That is not a capacity problem. That is a scheduling and workload-shaping problem. We are paying for idle silicon. Before we spend capital we cannot easily recover, I think we owe it to ourselves to understand whether the bottleneck is truly hardware or whether it is the way we are using what we have.

The cost asymmetry here is stark. A procurement decision commits us to a capital expenditure that will sit on the balance sheet for three to five years, depreciating whether or not we need it. If the underlying workload patterns shift — and they will, because our product roadmap is still evolving — we will be holding hardware optimised for a problem we no longer have. Utilisation improvements, by contrast, are almost entirely operational. They cost engineering time, which is expensive in its own way, but they do not lock us into a physical asset. If we improve scheduling, batch inference requests more aggressively, right-size model deployments, or introduce smarter caching, we can reverse those changes if they turn out to be wrong. Buying hardware is not reversible in any meaningful sense. You cannot un-buy a GPU cluster.

There is also an opportunity cost that I think we are underweighting. The engineering hours we would spend on procurement — evaluating vendors, negotiating, racking, networking, integrating, debugging driver issues, building monitoring for new nodes — are hours we are not spending on the utilisation work that might solve the same problem at lower cost. And those hours are not fungible in the way we sometimes pretend they are. The people best positioned to improve our scheduling and workload management are the same people who would be pulled into hardware integration if we go the procurement route.

I want to acknowledge the uncertainty here, because I do not think this is a slam dunk. There are scenarios where buying hardware is clearly correct. If we are approaching a hard ceiling on what software optimisation can achieve — if our models are simply too large, or our concurrency requirements are genuinely beyond what the current cluster can handle even at perfect utilisation — then no amount of clever scheduling will help, and we should buy. I am not certain we are not already at that ceiling. The utilisation numbers I cited are averages, and averages can hide tail behaviour that makes the cluster feel unusable even when it looks healthy on a dashboard.

My recommendation is this: we commit to a focused six-week utilisation sprint. We instrument the cluster properly, we identify the top three sources of waste, and we implement fixes. We set a clear success criterion — if we cannot bring peak-hour queue times below our target after that sprint, we reconvene and make the procurement decision with better data. This gives us a low-regret path. If we succeed, we have saved capital and built operational knowledge that compounds. If we fail, we have lost six weeks but gained the confidence that the hardware ceiling is real, and we proceed to buy with a clear conscience.

I would rather be wrong in a way that is cheap to correct than right in a way that was expensive to discover.

**MEMO: Hardware Procurement vs. Utilisation — A Recommendation**

**From:** Engineering Lead, Platform Infrastructure
**To:** Team, Product, Finance
**Re:** Should we buy more GPUs or get better at using the ones we have?

---

I want to put a recommendation on the table before we spend another week going in circles about this. The short version: we should invest the next two sprints in utilisation before we spend money on hardware. I'll explain why, and I'll be honest about where I'm uncertain.

Let me start with what we actually have. We own four A100 80GB nodes, which we acquired in two batches over the past eighteen months. They are not idle. They are not underutilised in the naive sense of sitting at 12% GPU utilisation while we wait for the next model to train. What they are is poorly scheduled. Our current queueing system treats every job as a monolith. A fine-tuning run that needs 40GB of VRAM blocks a node that could be serving inference for three other teams simultaneously. We have no preemption. We have no priority tiers. We have a first-in-first-out queue that rewards whoever submits a job at 6am and punishes everyone else.

The case for buying more hardware is not stupid. Latency matters to us in ways that are hard to quantify but easy to feel. When a product team wants to run an interactive evaluation loop—generate, score, regenerate, score again—the wall-clock time between iterations is what determines whether they can do ten experiments in an afternoon or two. Right now, if the queue is backed up, that afternoon becomes a day and a half. That is a real cost. It is not a line item on a spreadsheet, but it is the opportunity cost of every feature we don't ship because the team got bored waiting for results. I want to be clear that I take this seriously.

But here is what I keep coming back to. We have not yet exhausted the obvious wins. Our average GPU utilisation across the fleet, measured over the last thirty days, is 34%. That number is not a hardware problem. It is a scheduling problem, a fragmentation problem, and a cultural problem where teams submit jobs sized for worst-case memory rather than actual need. If we can get that number to 60% through better bin-packing, priority queues, and a modest amount of education around job sizing, we effectively gain two additional nodes without spending a dollar. That is not a marginal improvement. That is the difference between "we need to buy more" and "we don't need to buy more yet."

The reliability argument cuts both ways, and I want to acknowledge that. More hardware means more failure domains. A single node going down today blocks everything. Two nodes means we can tolerate one failure. But it also means more things to monitor, more firmware to update, more cooling to maintain, more of the operational surface area that has already consumed a disproportionate share of our time this quarter. We are a small team. Every new node is a new thing that will page someone at 3am. I think we are underestimating that tax.

On reversibility, this is where the asymmetry is sharpest. Improving utilisation is almost entirely reversible. If we build a better scheduler and it turns out we still need more capacity, we buy the hardware then, with better data, and the scheduler still helps. But buying hardware is not reversible in any meaningful sense. Once we order four more nodes, we own them for three to four years. We will be depreciating them, maintaining them, and justifying their existence long after the immediate pressure that motivated the purchase has passed. The cost of being wrong about utilisation is a few sprints of engineering time. The cost of being wrong about procurement is a quarter of a million dollars and a room full of equipment that becomes a sunk-cost anchor on future decisions.

I want to be transparent about my uncertainty. I could be wrong about the ceiling on utilisation. If our workloads are genuinely memory-bound in ways that no scheduler can fix—if we are hitting the physical limits of what four nodes can do for our current model sizes—then two more sprints of optimisation will just delay the inevitable purchase and add frustration. I don't think that's the case, but I can't prove it from the data I have today.

My recommendation: commit two sprints to a utilisation project with a clear success metric. If we cannot move fleet-wide GPU utilisation above 55% by the end of that window, we reconvene and buy. I think we will hit 55%. I think we will hit it and then some, and we will have bought ourselves another year of runway. But I want the decision to be data-driven, not vibes-driven, and I want us to have tried the cheap thing before we reach for the expensive one.
